title: Formal Reasoning and Decision Problems
question: Could following the rules of proof be left to a machine?

title: What exactly is a proof?
lead: Axioms are the chosen assumptions; rules of inference are the permitted steps.
takeaway: A proof is a finite object that a procedure can check. Checking shows the conclusion follows, not that the axioms are right.
notes: From P and “P implies Q” we may infer Q. Each edge records a dependency, not a passage of time.

title: Can the rules themselves be trusted?
lead: A system is consistent if it never proves both a statement and its opposite.
takeaway: Hilbert’s plan: make the rules explicit, then prove with reasoning about finite objects that they never give a contradiction.
notes: Even a statement about infinitely many numbers has a finite written proof, so proofs themselves can be studied mathematically.

title: When does a proof search stop?
question: List every candidate proof by length and check each one. When does this search finish?
answer: If a proof exists, eventually: it appears somewhere in the list. If none exists, never. No final candidate settles the matter.
notes: A decision procedure must do more than search: it must finish with a correct yes or no on every input.

title: Checking, searching, deciding
takeaway: To ask whether any procedure can decide, we need a precise account of what a procedure is.

title: Models of Computation
question: What exactly is a mechanical procedure?

title: Why is Euclid right, and why does it stop?
takeaway: Correctness: the gcd never changes (an invariant). Termination: the second entry keeps falling and cannot fall forever.
notes: These are separate arguments. Repeating the first pair forever would preserve the answer but never deliver it.

title: What must we record to resume a computation?
takeaway: A configuration is everything needed to continue; a run is a sequence of transitions between configurations.

title: Does the present determine the past?
question: In Euclid’s algorithm the next pair is determined. Is the previous one?
answer: No. Both \((30,18)\) and \((48,18)\) lead to \((18,12)\). Knowing how to continue does not tell us how to go back.

title: What counts as an elementary step?
lead: Break “divide” into steps that read a symbol, write one, move one cell, and change a finite state.
takeaway: A rule table is finite data, so one universal machine can read any program and simulate it.

title: Computability and Its Limits
question: Is there a question that no procedure can settle?

title: Is the Turing machine the right model?
takeaway: Equivalence of formal models is a theorem. That every effective method is a Turing machine is a thesis.
notes: The thesis is about what can be computed, not how fast. Quantum computers do not compute uncomputable functions; they can change the resources needed for computable ones.

title: Can one program predict whether every program halts?
steps: Suppose \(H(P,x)\) always halts and says whether \(P\) halts on \(x\).
Build \(D(p)\): if \(H(p,p)\) says “halts”, loop forever; otherwise stop.
If \(H(d,d)\) says “halts”, \(D\) loops. If it says “does not halt”, \(D\) stops.
Either answer is wrong, so no such \(H\) exists.
notes: This does not stop us analysing particular programs, or building analysers that sometimes answer “unknown”.

title: Two different limits
lead: Undecidability concerns procedures; incompleteness concerns what fixed axioms can settle.
takeaway: A consistent theory strong enough for arithmetic leaves some sentence undecided, and cannot prove its own consistency.
notes: These are the Gödel–Rosser theorem and Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem, stated here without proof. Their conditions matter.

title: From Computability to Reversibility
question: For problems we can solve, what does the solution do to the information it is given?

title: Does knowing the next step tell us the last?
takeaway: Deterministic means one successor. Reversible also needs one predecessor: the step must be one-to-one.

title: Must computing an answer lose the input?
takeaway: No: keep \((x,f(x))\). Even a many-to-one \(f\) can be computed without losing \(x\).
notes: Laws that govern isolated systems at small scales appear to run backward as well as forward. A computer built from such systems must compute without discarding information.

title: What we found
items: A proof is a finite object that a procedure can check.
Search finds proofs that exist but cannot decide every question.
Configurations and transitions make “procedure” precise; a universal machine runs them all.
Some questions, such as halting, are undecidable; strong theories are incomplete.
Reversibility asks whether a computation keeps the information it was given.
